Kitten thought the moon was a bowl of milk.' Students use multiple communication modes: they discuss orally with partners and share out to the whole group, and their ideas are captured in writing on the Unit 1 Guiding Question anchor chart.

However, students do not establish a purpose for a text they are constructing, and the knowledge of audience is not addressed.

clauses.clause: Evaluate the extent to which texts achieve their purposes based on author, audience, and context

verdicts.evidence: 'Why do you think Kevin Henkes wrote about the moon in this story?' (to imagine what the moon looks like to a kitten; to imagine what the kitten thinks when she looks at the moon)
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to (1) develop and apply knowledge of author, audience, and context to discern and establish the purpose of texts, and (2) evaluate the extent to which texts achieve those purposes. In Work Time B, students engage in the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol where they answer "'Why do you think Kevin Henkes wrote about the moon in this story?' (to imagine what the moon looks like to a kitten; to imagine what the kitten thinks when she looks at the moon)," demonstrating that students discern the author's purpose using knowledge of the author and story context. This partially meets the first clause because students discern purpose on the interpretation side but do not establish purpose for a text they construct, and audience knowledge is not addressed. The evaluate clause is not met: no activity asks students to judge how well the text achieves its purpose.
